questions.question: Development aid (official development assistance) is:
options: The transfer of money, goods, technology or expertise from wealthier countries and institutions to poorer ones, on terms gentler than the market's — grants or concessional loans
Any foreign investment that creates jobs
Loans at commercial interest rates
Trade agreements between rich and poor countries

questions.question: Aid pooled through the World Bank, UN agencies or the African Development Bank is called:
options: Bilateral aid
Multilateral aid — channelled through institutions that grant or lend it onward under shared rules
Non-governmental aid
Private investment

questions.question: Development co-operation differs from aid language because:
options: It involves larger sums of money
It excludes NGOs from participating
It frames a partnership with duties on both sides — the recipient sets priorities and accounts for results, and the donor funds the recipient's own plan
It applies only to emergency relief

questions.question: South Africa 'occupies both chairs at the table' because it:
options: Refuses all foreign assistance
Only donates and never receives
Channels all aid through the World Bank
Receives aid — notably health funding — while extending assistance in Africa through the African Renaissance Fund and joining trilateral projects

subtopics.title: Types of Aid: Technical, Conditional and Humanitarian

questions.question: Technical aid's great strength is permanence because:
options: Money is spent once but a transferred skill keeps producing for decades
Technical equipment never breaks down
It always involves the largest budgets
Experts remain in the country permanently

questions.question: Procurement tying means:
options: Aid must be repaid within a fixed period
The recipient must spend the aid on the donor's own goods and firms, so much of the money cycles home and costs inflate
Aid may only fund procurement of food
The recipient must match the aid with its own funds

questions.question: The structural adjustment era of the 1980s and 1990s is the classic case of:
options: Humanitarian aid delivered too slowly
Technical assistance without transfer
Policy conditionality — loans requiring spending cuts, privatisation and open markets, with the cuts falling on health and education in many African countries
Multilateral aid replacing bilateral aid

questions.question: Judging emergency food aid for failing to industrialise a country is a category error because:
options: Food aid always industrialises countries eventually
Industrialisation requires no external help
Emergency aid is never evaluated
Short-term relief stops the bleeding while long-term development aid builds the hospital — each tool has its own job

subtopics.title: When Aid Works: The Positive Case

questions.question: The strongest single piece of evidence that aid can work is:
options: The aid-funded vaccination campaign that eradicated smallpox — a disease deleted from the planet
The volume of aid disbursed each year
The number of donor agencies in existence
The growth of private investment in Africa

questions.question: In South Africa, Global Fund and PEPFAR financing contributed to:
options: The construction of new universities
The world's largest antiretroviral programme, with life expectancy climbing back from the low fifties to above sixty
The ending of load-shedding
A doubling of mineral exports

questions.question: Concessional finance matters for infrastructure because:
options: It carries the highest interest rates
It funds only urban projects
It builds the rural roads, water schemes and power lines that private capital will not risk
It replaces the need for any state planning

questions.question: Across the documented successes, aid works best when it is:
options: Spread thinly across as many sectors as possible
Delivered without consulting the recipient
Kept flowing permanently regardless of results
Aimed at a specific, measurable problem, aligned with the recipient's own priorities, and sustained long enough to finish the job

subtopics.title: When Aid Fails: Dependency, Distortion and Debt

questions.question: Aid dependency develops when:
options: Aid funds a large slice of the budget year after year, turning the state toward its donors and away from its citizens while the tax base stays unbuilt
A country receives aid during a single emergency
Aid is delivered through NGOs
Donors demand audited accounts

questions.question: Free food poured into functioning markets outside true emergencies causes distortion because:
options: It spoils before distribution
It undercuts local farmers until planting stops — solving this year's hunger by sowing next year's
It increases food prices for consumers
It cannot reach rural areas

questions.question: Through the 1980s and 1990s the debt trap meant that many African governments:
options: Refused to accept any further loans
Converted all loans into grants
Paid more in debt service than they spent on health and education combined — aid flowing backwards — until relief campaigns succeeded
Repaid their debts within a decade

questions.question: Fragmentation harms small recipient states because:
options: Aid arrives in currencies that cannot be exchanged
Donors refuse to fund small projects
Projects are always located in capitals
A small ministry drowns under hundreds of little donor projects, each demanding its own reports, vehicles and logos

subtopics.title: Fish, Fishing Lessons and the Flood

questions.question: In the proverb picture, the FISH stands for:
options: Humanitarian aid — food parcels, rescue boats and blankets, judged on speed and reach, but only able to feed today
Technical aid
Conditional aid
Private investment

questions.question: The fishing lesson usually beats the fish EXCEPT:
options: When the town has no river
In mid-flood, when a lesson is useless and a boat is everything — timing decides which aid is the right aid
When the lesson costs more than the fish
When the fishermen are already trained

questions.question: The beached boats at the end of the story represent:
options: A shortage of fishing equipment
The effects of overfishing
Dependency — free fish arriving forever until local fishermen cannot compete, and the town that fed itself waits on the truck
The benefits of imported food

questions.question: In the borehole story, having to buy the pump from the neighbour's shop at his price is:
options: Procurement tying — aid money cycling back to the donor's own companies while costs inflate
Policy conditionality
Multilateral pooling
A concessional loan

questions.question: The neighbour demanding a say in the household budget is the picture of:
options: Humanitarian principles
Policy conditionality — money flowing only if the recipient adopts prescribed policies, as in the structural adjustment era
Technical transfer
Development co-operation

questions.question: Recipients accept strings because:
options: Strings always improve project quality
International law requires acceptance
A dry borehole in a drought makes hard bargains look reasonable — urgent need weakens bargaining power
Donors offer no alternative forms of aid

questions.question: The co-operation upgrade to the gift-with-strings means:
options: The neighbour pays without any agreement
The household abandons its renovation
All conditions are simply removed
The household writes its own plan, the neighbour contributes to THAT plan, and both sign accountability agreements facing each other

questions.question: Entries on the triumphs pan of the scale include:
options: Smallpox eradicated, South Africa's ARV programme carried by Global Fund and PEPFAR money, malaria deaths cut, and rapid flood and earthquake relief
Structural adjustment and tied aid invoices
The debt service of the 1980s
Fragmented donor projects

questions.question: Entries on the failures pan carry mechanisms such as:
options: Vaccines working too slowly
Free food beaching local farmers, loans becoming budget-eating debt, strings routing money home, dependency, corruption and fragmentation
Roads built in the wrong provinces
Nurses trained in the wrong specialities

questions.question: The scaffolding verdict says aid works when it:
options: Remains in place permanently as the economy's frame
Replaces the state's own construction
Targets a specific finishable job, follows the recipient's own plan, and is designed from day one to make itself unnecessary
Avoids all measurable targets

questions.question: A plain yes or no to 'does aid work?' fails because:
options: The evidence is too thin to answer
Aid statistics are secret
The question is unanswerable in principle
Both pans of the scale hold documented cases — the honest answer weighs triumphs and failures and names the variables that decide between them
